Skill Is Not Document: A Query-Conditional Benchmark and Two-Stage Retriever for LLM Agent Skill Routing

Zifei Wang Affiliation: Tencent IMA Product Center Email: zifeiwang@tencent.com    Wei Wen Affiliation: Tencent Youtu Lab Email: jawnrwen@tencent.com    Qiang Ji Affiliation: Tencent IMA Product Center Email: peasirji@tencent.com    Ruizhi Qiao Affiliation: Tencent IMA Product Center Affiliation: Tencent Youtu Lab Email: ruizhiqiao@tencent.com    Xing Sun Affiliation: Tencent IMA Product Center Affiliation: Tencent Youtu Lab Email: winfredsun@tencent.com
Abstract

LLM agents complete complex tasks by composing multiple skills, and skill retrieval is a front-end stage for agents. Skill retrieval differs fundamentally from traditional document retrieval at the supervision level: top-KK joint correctness depends not only on the semantic relevance of each individual query–skill pair, but also on whether the skills retrieved together can collaborate to fulfill the task under the given query. Such “skill compatibility” cannot be derived from independent relevance alone. Yet existing LLM-based data synthesis pipelines can produce a direct supervision signal for “which skills should not be jointly retrieved under this query”—namely the LLM’s own rejection decisions—and this signal is routinely discarded as low-quality data. To address this gap, we propose Reject-as-Resource Retriever (R3) and construct R3-Skill, a bilingual (Chinese–English) skill retrieval benchmark targeting realistic agent skill routing. R3-Skill spans four language directions, features query phrasings close to real user requests, and is verified through multi-expert cross-checking. The dataset contains 10,246 skills grouped into 8 thematic super-domains; 41,592 accepted queries; and 32,828 LLM-rejected annotations, further organized into an 8-class rejection-reason taxonomy. Unlike prior datasets, R3-Skill keeps the rejection signal that is usually thrown away, and uses it as negative supervision for compatibility. On R3-Skill, we build a two-stage retrieval system comprising R3-Embedding and R3-Reranker, with skill compatibility incorporated as an explicit training signal. A gradient-level analysis is provided: in the bi-encoder, the representation of any single skill is jointly determined by multiple queries, so the “push-away” gradient injected by the compatibility signal is diluted by bilateral balancing and contributes little at the recall stage; in the cross-encoder, however, each query–skill pair is scored independently, allowing the compatibility signal to be used as graded supervision for ranking without loss. We therefore place the compatibility signal at the cross-encoder stage, and ablation studies on two datasets confirm this choice. The R3-Embedding + R3-Reranker pipeline attains Hit@1 = 0.7714, NDCG@10 = 0.8327 and Set-Compat = 0.3525 on R3-Skill. The dataset, training code and model weights are released as open source for agent skill routing.

1 Introduction

1.1 LLM Agents and Skills

Over the past year, agent systems have moved from early ReAct Yao et al. (2023), which interleaves reasoning and tool calls into a trajectory, and Toolformer Schick et al. (2023), which enables models to learn API calls in a self-supervised manner, toward a higher-level reusable unit—the skill. In October 2025, Anthropic formalized the Agent Skills specification  (2025), packaging what used to be scattered prompt templates, function wrappers and documentation snippets into a directory containing a SKILL.md file with metadata, a body, and supporting scripts, all loaded on demand at inference time. Skills have since been adopted by major agent platforms such as Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI, and the community has accumulated tens to hundreds of thousands of skills within months Anthropic (2025). Recent surveys Xu and Yan (2026); Jiang et al. (2026) position skills as the third paradigm of agent capability extension, following prompt engineering and tool use. A skill and a tool are not the same kind of object: a tool is an atomic “input →\to call →\to output” function, whereas a skill teaches the agent how to handle a class of problems—covering call constraints, multi-step procedures, canonical code and edge cases  (2025); Xu and Yan (2026). Memento-Skills Zhou et al. (2026) further shows that, when the skill library is treated as continuously updatable agent memory, improvements to the skills themselves yield 26.2% / 116.2% relative accuracy gains on GAIA / HLE respectively. Completing a complex task typically requires several skills working together—for example, “transcribe this meeting recording and then summarize the key takeaways” calls for a speech-to-text skill followed by a summarization skill, and a missing or mismatched skill can cause the task to fail.

What does a skill look like?

A typical skill contains:

  • •

    name: a short identifier, e.g. SendGrid Email Send;

  • •

    description: a one-line purpose, e.g. “Send transactional emails through SendGrid”;

  • •

    body: detailed call instructions (API shape, parameter constraints, platform dependencies, best practices, canonical code), typically tens to hundreds of lines.

1.2 Why Skill Retrieval Matters

The intuitive approach is to place all skills in the prompt and let the LLM choose. This is not viable in real agent deployments:

(A) The skill inventory keeps growing. Public skill repositories have expanded from ~36K skills indexed by SkillFlow Tagkopoulos et al. (2025), ~26K in SRA-Bench Su et al. (2026), and 280K+ reported by AgentSkillOS Li et al. (2026a), to even larger public corpora. As skill counts grow from dozens to thousands or tens of thousands, an “all-prompt” approach runs into three problems: token cost, inference latency and context-length limits. Prior work also shows the limits of injecting full skill sets directly into the inference context: this approach brings in large amounts of irrelevant context, and the model can only use these skills while reading them, rather than absorbing them as its own capability Lu et al. (2026). Empirical token-length measurements on R3-Skill (Figure 1) show a long-tailed distribution; injecting the entire library at once already exceeds the single-call context window of mainstream inference services.

(B) Skills are highly similar; descriptions alone do not separate them. Take transactional email skills: SendGrid, Mailgun and Postmark are independent skills but their descriptions are almost identical—“Send transactional emails”. The differences are buried in the body: SendGrid emphasizes enterprise-scale, high-throughput infrastructure; Mailgun highlights developer flexibility and webhook callbacks; Postmark physically isolates transactional and marketing email to protect deliverability (Message Streams). When a user asks “isolate marketing from transactional email while preserving deliverability”, the retriever must read the body to pick Postmark. Prior work validates this directly on a ~80K skill pool: hiding the skill body lowers routing accuracy by 31–44 percentage points Zheng et al. (2026), indicating that the body is not just metadata but the main routing signal.

(C) Multi-skill routing demands “minimal yet sufficient”. For each query, the agent needs precisely the right set of skills: missing a key skill makes the task unsolvable, while including a conflicting skill introduces failure modes of its own. SkillsBench provides a direct quantification: curated skills improve overall pass rate by +16.2pp, but 16 of 84 tasks show performance regressions Li et al. (2026b); Skills in the Wild further reports diminishing returns under more realistic settings Liu et al. (2026); CoEvoSkills also observes that human-authored skills bring substantially uneven gains across domains, with clear regressions in some Zhang et al. (2026). The retriever must therefore not just return candidates but rank them reliably—positions in the top-KK shape downstream call success.

(D) Sandbox provisioning cost in real deployments. In production agent platforms, concurrent users typically share an agent through per-session sandboxes: a sandbox is created when a user starts a session and is reclaimed by a periodic sweep after the session has been idle for some time, so a one-sandbox-per-user model is infeasible. Each sandbox must install the skills it actually needs before the agent can run. If every sandbox loads the full skill library, the install / reset latency grows roughly linearly with the library size and quickly dominates the user-perceived cold-start time. Routing only the KK skills each sandbox actually needs is therefore an engineering requirement, not just a quality issue.

1.3 Skill Retrieval ≠\neq Document Retrieval

Document retrieval typically assumes that “two documents being retrieved together for the same query” is harmless—if both are relevant, returning them together introduces no error. Skill retrieval is different. What is returned is a set of capabilities the agent will actually invoke. Whether two skills can run together under a particular query depends on the query itself; a different query over the same pair can flip the verdict. “Whether two skills should be jointly retrieved” is therefore not a global binary relation between skills, but must be assessed under a given query. Concurrent work Skill-RAG also points out that the bottleneck of many hard cases in RAG lies not in missing evidence but in a structural alignment gap between the query and the evidence space, which motivates its post-hoc skill selection mechanism Wei et al. (2026). We focus on the retrieval stage itself: in the training objective, “relevance” should depend on the specific query rather than be determined by the skill alone. We now formalize skill compatibility.

One pair of skills, two queries, opposite verdicts.

Take A: Terraform IaC and B: AUR Package Publish:

  • •

    query1: “Package an internal tool, publish it to a Linux software repository, and set up an IaC pipeline”—both A and B should be jointly retrieved.

  • •

    query2: “Set up basic test infrastructure for the team”—only A is needed; B is unrelated to the intent.

Formalization (modeling decomposition).

Given a query qq and the target skill set Sq∗⊆𝒮S_{q}^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{S}, we decompose the probability of jointly retrieving Sq∗S_{q}^{*} in the top-KK into two factors:

Pr⁡[Sq∗⊆top-​K∣q]≈∏s∈Sq∗Pr⁡[s∈top-​K∣q]⏟relevance⋅C⁡(q,Sq∗)⏟skill compatibility\Pr[\,S_{q}^{*}\subseteq\text{top-}K\mid q\,]\;\approx\;\underbrace{\prod_{s\in S_{q}^{*}}\Pr[\,s\in\text{top-}K\mid q\,]}_{\text{relevance}}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{C(q,S_{q}^{*})}_{\text{skill compatibility}}

The first factor is the product of per-skill recall probabilities, mirroring the implicit assumption of document retrieval: documents are mutually independent, so “both are retrieved” is equivalent to multiplying the two individual probabilities. The second factor C⁡(q,Sq∗)∈ℝ≥0C(q,S_{q}^{*})\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} captures skill compatibility: C=1C=1 reduces to the classical assumption (the skills do not affect each other); C<1C<1 means that even though every member is independently a plausible candidate, the set conflicts under query qq—e.g. overlapping functionality, inconsistent style, or incompatible ecosystems—and should not be jointly retrieved; C>1C>1 means the opposite, that the skills mutually reinforce each other under qq. Document retrieval can be approximated by C≡1C\equiv 1; in skill retrieval, CC depends strongly on the query and tends to be far from 1 in multi-skill scenarios.

Training on relevance alone is not enough: a skill ranking high on its own does not mean the retrieved set is jointly executable, so compatibility needs its own supervision signal. We estimate an empirical proxy for this constraint on real data in §2.3.

1.4 Status Quo and Gaps in Skill Retrieval Datasets

Adding skill compatibility into the training objective is mainly limited by the lack of suitable training data. Existing skill retrieval datasets fall roughly into two categories: (i) end-to-end task benchmarks—SkillsBench Li et al. (2026b), SRA-Bench Su et al. (2026), SkillFlow Tagkopoulos et al. (2025)—which mainly target the post-retrieval incorporation/application stage and lack the scale to train a retriever; (ii) training resources designed specifically for skill retrieval Zheng et al. (2026); Cho et al. (2026). Both inherit the contrastive paradigm from document retrieval (the DPR Karpukhin et al. (2020) / ANCE Xiong et al. (2020) / RocketQA Qu et al. (2021) line, with BM25 Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) as a sparse baseline) and are fairly mature on document retrieval. Toward the goal of agent skill routing, however, three gaps remain:

  1. 1.

    LLM rejection signal is discarded. Existing query–skill synthesis pipelines drop a sample as soon as the LLM judges a skill set “not naturally combinable”—yet this is precisely where compatibility-oriented negatives are densest.

  2. 2.

    Cross-lingual coverage is lacking. Existing skill retrieval resources cover English only Cho et al. (2026); Zheng et al. (2026). Cluster analysis of 26,502 public skills on the ClawHub platform by Red Skills or Blue Skills shows that English skills lean toward capability modules while Chinese skills lean toward scenario packaging Hu et al. (2026)—meaning that the linguistic asymmetry of “a Chinese query retrieving English skills” is worse in real deployments. While multilingual retrievers (e.g. BGE-M3 Chen et al. (2024)) achieve query–document-level Chinese–English alignment, existing datasets still do not provide a training signal for cross-lingual skill compatibility under given queries.

  3. 3.

    Test-set query phrasing diverges from real user requests. Queries generated by LLMs under structured prompts tend to be overly long, written in formal register, and dense with technical terms, letting retrievers lean on lexical keywords for inflated scores. Skills in the Wild reports a similar phenomenon: when the agent must self-retrieve from a 34k real skill pool with progressively more realistic test settings, pass rate drops with difficulty and approaches a no-skill baseline at the strictest setting Liu et al. (2026).

This work targets the three gaps above: we build R3-Skill, retain LLM-judged non-co-executable samples as supervision for skill compatibility, cover four query language directions across Chinese and English, and apply LLM rewriting to the test queries to better resemble real user requests. On top of this dataset we train two retrieval models, R3-Embedding and R3-Reranker.

1.5 Contributions

Our contributions:

  • •

    C1 (theory): a formal decomposition of top-KK joint correctness in skill retrieval into a relevance factor and a skill-compatibility factor, with a geometric analysis of injecting the SKIP signal into a dual-encoder provided in the appendix.

  • •

    C2 (data): R3-Skill, a benchmark with 10,246 skills, 41,592 accepted queries, and 32,828 SKIP annotations, covering 4 query language directions and 6 query styles, with test queries close to real user requests and verified by multiple experts.

  • •

    C3 (method): a two-stage retrieval system—R3-Embedding trained with standard InfoNCE; R3-Reranker, on a cross-encoder, encodes SKIP partners as a graded label and optimizes ranking directly via a listwise CE objective.

  • •

    C4 (empirical): we open-source the two-stage models R3-Embedding and R3-Reranker, achieving Hit@1 = 0.7714, NDCG@10 = 0.8327 and Set-Compat = 0.3525 on R3-Skill, available for use in agent skill routing.

2 R3-Skill Dataset

2.1 Reject as Resource

Existing skill–query synthesis pipelines have the LLM evaluate the plausibility of a skill combination and discard the sample on a None verdict. R3-Skill turns this into a WRITE / SKIP decision: the WRITE branch produces a query, the SKIP branch retains the entire record, and both are stored in parallel. The quality of the SKIP signal depends mainly on prompt design; we defer the full set of prompts to Appendix D.

Conventional pipeline
verdict = LLM(skill_set)
if verdict == WRITE:
    save (skill_set, query)
else:              # SKIP
    discard sample  # signal lost R3-Skill pipeline
verdict = LLM(skill_set)
if verdict == WRITE:
    save (skill_set, query)
else:              # SKIP
    save as negative

2.2 Skill Pool

We collect 95,212 raw skills from public agent-skill repositories on GitHub, covering both Chinese and English. These skills exhibit substantial cross-source forking and mirroring; after exact-hash deduplication across sources and removal of pure file-operation entries, a clean pool of 10,246 skills remains.

2.3 Near-Neighbor Hard-Constraint Sampling

Sampling skill combinations uniformly at random produces SKIP instances that are mostly easy: two skills are completely unrelated and trivially distinguishable without any training. Learning skill compatibility requires harder negatives: semantically similar skill combinations that nevertheless cannot be jointly executed under the query. We encode skill text with BGE-M3 Chen et al. (2024) and run KMeans for K∈{10,20,30,40}K\in\{10,20,30,40\}, comparing parameter choices via clustering quality and human spot-checking; we settle on K=40K=40, then merge the 40 sub-clusters into 8 super-domains. Cluster quality curves across KK and the K=40K=40 hierarchy of 8 super-domains ×\times 40 sub-clusters are deferred to Figures 5 and 6 in the appendix. Sampling uses the two-level structure: k=1k=1 samples freely; k=2k=2 requires the two skills to come from the same sub-cluster; k=3k=3 requires the three skills to come from the same super-domain. On all 41,592 queries, the k=2k=2 same-sub-cluster rate and k=3k=3 same-super-domain rate are both 100%; the LLM judges only 56.3% of k=2k=2 and 36.5% of k=3k=3 combinations as jointly executable, an empirical proxy for the compatibility-constraint strength C⁡(q,Sq∗)C(q,S_{q}^{*}) in the formalization of §1.3.

2.4 LLM Annotation and Reject Reason Taxonomy

Each candidate skill combination is sent to the LLM for a WRITE / SKIP decision (k=1k=1 generates a query directly; k≥2k\geq 2 triggers the full judgment). The WRITE branch generates queries in 6 styles—task_direct, scene, role_setup, constraint, multi_step, debug—approximately uniformly distributed across the 4 directions, with length statistics shown in the appendix C. The complete annotation flow diagram and the full set of generation prompts (4 directions ×\times {single, multi}, 8 templates in total) appear in Appendix D and Figure 7.

Training-set queries and SKIP annotations are produced by DeepSeek-V4-Pro DeepSeek-AI (2026); test-set queries and ground-truth labels are drafted by Qwen3-235B-A22B Yang et al. (2025) and verified by multiple experts.

Rejection-reason taxonomy.

We keep SKIP as negative supervision rather than discard it. We apply rule-based heuristics to 15,962 SKIP samples and build an 8-class rejection-reason taxonomy. The rules try to match a specific cause first and fall back to forced_chaining (which captures common Chinese “forced stacking” verdicts) at the end; rule coverage is 93.3%, with the remaining 6.7% routed to the unknown class. Rejection patterns differ structurally between Chinese and English directions: en2en is dominated by domain mismatch, while en2zh focuses on the “forced stacking” verdicts typical of Chinese LLM expression. The en2zh k=3k=3 SKIP rate reaches 80.9%—the cross-lingual setting makes it harder for the LLM to accept a combination as plausible Hu et al. (2026); even under the strictest constraints, SKIP still accounts for 63.5%, i.e. over 60% of three-skill combinations among BGE-M3 nearest neighbors are incompatible. The full taxonomy, by-direction stacked-bar distributions, and representative WRITE / SKIP examples are deferred to Appendix C.

The dataset is split at the skill-pool level so that train_pool and test_pool share no skill, yielding four release artifacts: train.jsonl with 30,287 training queries, test_hard.jsonl with 5,696 test queries, skip_train.jsonl with 9,300 training SKIPs, and skip_eval.jsonl with 16,365 SKIPs for auxiliary evaluation. All rule sets, taxonomy hits and final released data are spot-checked by multiple experts, with hit accuracy ≥99%\geq 99\%.

2.5 Comparison with Existing Skill Datasets

3 Method

R3-Skill provides two kinds of supervision: WRITE indicates a skill set that can complete a task under some query; SKIP indicates a skill set that was sampled together but judged by the LLM as unable to co-occur naturally. We train a two-stage pipeline: R3-Embedding (bi-encoder, fine-tuned from Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B Yang et al. (2025)) does coarse recall over the full skill pool; R3-Reranker (cross-encoder, fine-tuned from Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B Yang et al. (2025)) reranks the recalled candidates.

Stage 1 — R3-Embedding (Bi-encoder).

We use standard InfoNCE training van den Oord et al. (2018); for each query, the candidate pool consists of the GT s+s^{+} and nn BM25 hard negatives {sj−}\{s^{-}_{j}\}:

ℒemb​(q)=−log⁡exp⁡(𝐞​(q)⊤​𝐞​(s+)/τ)∑c∈{s+}∪{sj−}exp⁡(𝐞​(q)⊤​𝐞​(c)/τ).\mathcal{L}_{\text{emb}}(q)=-\log\frac{\exp(\mathbf{e}(q)^{\top}\mathbf{e}(s^{+})/\tau)}{\sum_{c\in\{s^{+}\}\cup\{s^{-}_{j}\}}\exp(\mathbf{e}(q)^{\top}\mathbf{e}(c)/\tau)}.

Stage 2 — R3-Reranker (Cross-encoder).

For each query, the candidate pool consists of the GT, SKIP partners, and top-ranked candidates from R3-Embedding, padded to 10 candidates; we adopt graded ListNet:

label(s)={3,s∈Sq∗1,s​ is a SKIP partner0,otherwise,ℒrrk(q)=−∑syslogps,\text{label}(s)=\begin{cases}3,&s\in S_{q}^{*}\\ 1,&s\text{ is a SKIP partner}\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases},\quad\mathcal{L}_{\text{rrk}}(q)=-\sum_{s}y_{s}\log p_{s},

where ysy_{s} is obtained from the labels via softmax normalization, and psp_{s} is the softmax of the reranker scores. The intermediate level (label = 1) assigned to SKIP partners only adjusts the relative ordering inside the training candidate pool; SKIP partners are not counted as GT at evaluation time. The two-stage evaluation protocol is: R3-Embedding recalls the top-20, then R3-Reranker reranks within that candidate set. We explain why SKIP partners are not injected at the embedding stage in Appendix B.

4 Experiments

4.1 Evaluation Setup

We use two benchmarks: the R3-Skill test set and the SkillRet official test set Cho et al. (2026). In addition to the standard metrics Hit@1 / NDCG / R@K / Comp@K, we introduce a metric Set-Compat: computed only on queries with |G​T|≥2|GT|\geq 2, scoring 1 iff Sq∗⊆top-​mS_{q}^{*}\subseteq\text{top-}m (with m=|G​T|m=|GT|), to measure whether the entire GT set is retrieved into the top-mm positions simultaneously. Other evaluation details are in Appendix A.

4.2 Embedding
